findings.title: Removal of public findMany() is a breaking change for existing callers
findings.body: This change deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method (which previously merged the caller's `where`/`select`/pagination with auth+filter conditions and returned rows) and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a raw SQL fragment. Any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService` that calls `service.findMany({ where, select, take, ... })` (e.g. the insights tRPC router or other server code) will now fail to compile or silently have no equivalent one-call API, because the caller must instead build its own `$queryRaw`/Prisma query and manually AND the returned fragment into a WHERE clause. The PR only touches the service and its test file, so it does not demonstrate that all call sites were migrated. A maintainer should verify there are no remaining `findMany` callers (and that the caller side now executes raw SQL correctly) before merging.

findings.title: Only DB-executing test checks a positive match, no negative/authorization-exclusion assertion
findings.body: The single test that actually runs SQL against `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` (the `getBaseConditions` case) only asserts that the expected user's booking is returned. For a change explicitly flagged as high-risk authorization logic, there is no test asserting that data belonging to other users/teams/orgs is *excluded* by the generated SQL (e.g. a booking owned by a different user in the same org, a team booking outside the requested team, or a non-owner/member's org data). Without a negative case, a subtle mistake in the AND/OR parenthesization or in the `isTeamBooking`/`teamId` predicates would pass tests while leaking data. Add at least one test that creates a booking the caller must NOT see and asserts the raw query returns nothing for it.

findings.title: Public condition builders return unparenthesized OR fragments that are unsafe to compose with AND
findings.body: `buildFilterConditions` (line 106) and the org/team authorization builders (lines 164-174, 196-207) return fragments such as `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` or `(teamCond) OR (userCond)` without wrapping the whole expression in parentheses when there is a single element (or when the OR is the resulting top-level expression). `getBaseConditions` currently wraps these as `(${auth}) AND (${filter})`, so it is safe today, but these methods are public (`getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`). Any caller that composes a returned fragment with `AND`/`OR` without adding its own parentheses will get wrong precedence — e.g. `(A) OR (B) AND x` evaluates as `(A) OR ((B) AND x)`. The tests now assert the unparenthesized strings, locking in the fragile contract. Return fully parenthesized, self-contained predicates so fragments are safe to concatenate.

findings.title: Org-scope test asserts an array whose order is not guaranteed by the query
findings.body: The org-scope assertion compares the generated SQL values array against `[testData.user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. These ids come from `Array.from(new Set(userIdsFromOrg))`, where `userIdsFromOrg` is obtained from `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds` with no `ORDER BY`. Postgres may return membership rows in any order, so the `.values` array (and the teams array) can differ between runs, making this assertion flaky. Sort the ids before asserting, or assert set membership rather than exact array order.

findings.title: Caching tests removed while caching logic remains
findings.body: This PR deletes the entire `describe("Caching")` block that verified `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions` reuse `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions`. The caching fields and the `=== undefined` guards in the service are unchanged, so the removed tests leave that behavior uncovered. Since the caching was previously exercised, restore equivalent tests (second call returns the same cached `Prisma.Sql`) rather than dropping the coverage.
